title: Matthew Hopkins East Anglian Witch-Hunt: Largest English Persecution
description: Matthew Hopkins, self-styled 'Witch-Finder General,' conducted the most intense witch prosecution in English history between 1645 and 1647, resulting in the execution of approximately 100-120 people across Essex, Suffolk, Norfolk, Huntingdonshire, and neighboring counties during the disruption of the Civil War. Hopkins used techniques including sleep deprivation ('watching'), the swimming test, and searching for witch marks to extract confessions, operating under contract with local authorities. His methods were controversial even at the time; he published The Discovery of Witches (1647) to defend his procedures against critics. Hopkins died in 1647, reportedly of tuberculosis, though later legend said he was himself swum as a witch.
historiographical_note: Malcolm Gaskill's Witchfinders: A Seventeenth-Century English Tragedy (2005) is the definitive modern study, situating Hopkins within the social breakdown of the English Civil War. James Sharpe had earlier analyzed the East Anglian persecution as an exception to the general English pattern of moderate prosecution — significant precisely because the conditions that enabled it (judicial vacuum, war disruption, disrupted oversight) were exceptional rather than normal.
source_method: Hopkins, The Discovery of Witches (1647); assize records; Gaskill, Witchfinders (2005); secondary scholarship
